reference_opening.argument: This video is non-scam content because it primarily explains XRP, including how it may be bought and stored, while presenting itself as educational rather than direct buy or sell advice. Although it promotes passive-income training and coaching, it warns of possible total loss, disclaims licensed-advisor status, and does not promise profits. The merchant-processing form and request to comment are described as separate commercial or audience-engagement elements without established deception, required payment, or a causal route to wealth.

opening.argument: The video links an income outcome to a concrete external action, not merely to neutral background education. It says the speaker released training showing viewers how to earn passive income on XRP and other assets through the first description link, while the description repeats that invitation. The later call-to-action escalates this into booking a one-on-one strategy call to learn how to earn passive income. In context, XRP is also presented as something viewers can buy, hold, and build into a portfolio. That is a participation pathway connecting crypto involvement and directed clicks or calls with a promised holding-related income benefit.

rebuttal.rebuttal: Calling the material educational does not answer the specific income solicitation. The cited XRP explanation establishes a topic, and the wallet instructions establish mechanics, but neither explains why viewers are directed to a training link and a one-on-one call in connection with passive income. The disclaimer says there are no guarantees; it does not remove the income-oriented invitation or the route into the promoted program.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The quotes show an invitation to educational material, not a promise that clicking or booking produces profit. The speaker expressly says the content is not financial advice and warns that crypto can result in loss. The argument also fails to show that the viewer must buy XRP, pay for the training, or receive any return; it treats a general passive-income topic as proof of a token-return scheme.

No Guarantees: We don’t promise profits

opening.argument: Several risk signals appear together: crypto participation, a passive-income claim, an external link, coaching, and stated scarcity. The on-screen promotion pairs “EARN PASSIVE INCOME” with “Watch Free Training Below” and advertises “5-Month 1-1 Coaching” and “Passive Crypto Income.” The speaker also says calendar spots are limited and directs viewers to check back if no call is available. Meanwhile, the description places the income offer alongside XRP trading links. Even without inventing a guaranteed percentage or a specific mechanism, this combination frames crypto-related participation as a route to passive returns and uses urgency to move viewers toward an external offer.

citations.quote: we have limited spots on the calendar available because every single time I drop a video on this channel, the spots fill up pretty quick
you want to learn how to earn passive income on your XRP and other assets, then click the link in the description below
Buy, Sell, & Trade XRP Here

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense isolates the warnings while omitting the promotional combination visible and audible in the same presentation. “No guarantees” is a legal qualification, not evidence that the passive-income pitch, external funnel, coaching offer, and limited-calendar language are unrelated. The issue is the pressure and framing surrounding crypto returns, not whether a precise return figure was stated.

citations.quote: No Guarantees: We don’t promise profits
the spots fill up pretty quick

true_side_reply.rebuttal: These signals remain compatible with ordinary marketing for education and optional coaching. The frame does not establish a return, a required purchase, or a false claim, and the calendar statement does not prove fabricated scarcity. The description explicitly warns that crypto trading carries extreme risks and that past performance is not predictive, which undercuts the claim that the presentation promises passive returns.

citations.quote: Crypto trading carries extreme risks, including total loss
Past performance isn’t predictive
Affiliate links may earn commissions

opening.argument: The educational wrapper functions as promotion because the lesson repeatedly moves viewers toward participation. After explaining XRP, the speaker gives step-by-step purchase instructions, recommends starting with a dollar amount, promotes a training for passive income, and offers a call with the speaker or team. The program is not a peripheral mention: the speaker says the team helps people build crypto portfolios and invites viewers to learn what the top one percent are doing. Thus, the beginner lesson supplies credibility and a buying context for a crypto-income funnel, rather than operating solely as detached education.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense calls the purchase and storage material proof of education, but operational instructions can also make promotion actionable. The speaker does not stop at explaining XRP: he recommends an entry amount, directs viewers to training and a team call, and connects that funnel to passive income. The disclaimer does not change the functional progression from learning, to buying, to pursuing returns.

citations.quote: step number three is just buy XRP

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The presence of purchase instructions does not establish that the lesson deceptively promotes appreciation or dividends. It explains exchange use, custody, volatility, diversification, and dollar-cost averaging, while repeatedly limiting the recommendation to money the viewer can afford to lose. The cited “top 1%” phrase shows aspirational marketing, but not a promised return or a required crypto purchase.
